newsitem.title: THAILAND: INSTANT VIEW - Thai economic package.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Thai economic package.

text.p: Thailand announced a series of tough measures on Tuesday, including the suspension of 42 ailing finance firms, to boost the country's beleaguered economy and satisfy International Monetary Fund (IMF) requirements in order to obtain economic aid.
Thailand also set targets of maintaining $25 billion in foreign reserves, cutting the current account deficit, controlling inflation and hiking the value added tax.
Following are comments from analysts and economists.
NOBUO NAKAYAMA, JOINT GENERAL MANAGER OF SAKURA BANK LTD
"I felt that the number of finance firms being suspended was too high. I wonder what kind of standards were used in making the decision."

"I don't think this will be enough, as there are still many uncertain points to be worked out concerning the troubled finance firms...As for macro-economic policy targets, I think they are mostly in line with our expectations."
"The Thai government must strive to carry out these measures and explain the policy effects in order to send a clear message to assure the financial markets.

"I believe the government still needs to mull details and work out action programmes to ensure these measures will be surely in place. I think it would take some more time before (the) rescue package for Thailand will be finalised."
CHAN CHIA LIN, HEAD OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH AT ABN-AMRO BANK IN SINGAPORE
She said the measures announced by the Thai government held few surprises but would be seen as positive in the long run.

"In terms of the aim to balance the budget, raise the value-added tax and to try to bring the current account deficit down, they were in large part expected by the market. But it's quite positive that the cabinet appears to have approved these measures."

"What was surprising was the closure of the 42 finance firms. In the longer term, there's no doubt it's positive for the finance sector. The government is sending a clear signal that it will not bail out the weaker ones and that would be an IMF condition. But the immediate impact is going to be negative for the stock market and unless the government comes out to reassure the public that it stands behind depositors, we could see nervousness and depositors withdrawing money from the other financial institutions."
CHAING YAO CHYE, HEAD OF ASIA PACIFIC RESEARCH AT CIBC IN SINGAPORE.
"The (three percentage point) VAT rise was pretty much as expected and I think it's good because they really have to shore up the revenue side of their fiscal balance."
"VAT is a good way to do it, if you want to tighten your belt via the consumption side."
"The suspension of the finance companies is a surprise in terms of timing in as much as they are so many of them in one go. And we still haven't heard what has happened to the other 16."
DAVID CONNER, HEAD OF RESEARCH AT INDOSUEZ WI CARR SECURITIES
"I think this clearly looks like a big step towards the ultimate adoption of an IMF structural reform package and I think that mostly explains why the market has shrugged it off.
"It will ultimamtely pave the way for a stronger financial system in the future and that is good news for the stock market, and good news for Thailand," he said.

"In the short term there are some negative elements. The number of companies suspended, 42 in addition to the original 16, and the amount of financing provided to these companies... suggest the magnitude of a problem greater than observers expected."
"I think most observers already had very dire expectations of the overall magnitude of the problem, this basically exceeds our expectations of the problems.@
Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said finance firms had borrowed 430 billion baht from the central bank to ease their liquidity problems. ($1 = 31 baht)
